summaries.example: Maya notices that her classmate is speaking. She waits, listens, and does not laugh at a mistake. She is showing respect by paying attention and treating the other student as someone whose thoughts matter. Respect does not always mean agreeing. It can mean taking a person seriously.
summaries.summary: Respect is a way of taking someone or something seriously and responding appropriately. It may appear in behavior, such as following a speed limit, or in an attitude, such as seeing another person as worthy of attention. Philosophers ask what can deserve respect, why it deserves it, and what respect asks us to do. A major idea is respect for persons: every person may deserve basic respect simply as a person. This is different from admiration, which may be earned by excellent actions. Respect can also mean being careful around something powerful, obeying a rule, honoring a role, or caring for nature. Self-respect means valuing yourself and protecting your worth. The entry explains that people do not agree about all these questions, but respect matters in friendships, schools, workplaces, laws, communities, and public life.
key_ideas: Respect can be shown through actions, feelings, attention, and choices.
People may respect rules, other people, nature, traditions, or someone’s rights.
Some respect is earned by good actions, but many philosophers think every person deserves basic moral respect.
Self-respect and respect for others are connected, and unfair treatment can damage self-respect.
Philosophers disagree about exactly what deserves respect and what respectful behavior requires.
summaries.why_it_matters: Respect helps people live together without treating one another as objects or as worthless. It can guide listening, fairness, safety, and responsible disagreement. Self-respect can help people stand up against degrading treatment and pursue worthwhile goals. Thinking carefully about respect also helps us notice when a rule, custom, or polite action may still be unfair or harmful.

important_terms.definition: Treating someone or something as important and responding in a fitting way.
The value people have simply because they are persons, not because they are famous, talented, or successful.
Respecting yourself by understanding that you matter and should not accept treatment that makes you seem worthless.
A careful way of noticing and responding to something instead of ignoring it.

questions_to_think_about: Can you respect someone’s opinion without agreeing with it?
Is following a rule always the same as having a respectful attitude?
What kinds of actions help a person keep self-respect?
Should animals or nature receive some form of respect?
Can someone do a polite action without truly being respectful?

summaries.example: Suppose a student asks a teammate to share private information for a project. The teammate refuses. Respecting the teammate does not require liking the decision or abandoning the project; it requires recognizing the teammate as an agent who may make decisions about personal information, and not using pressure or deception to obtain it. The student may still explain the project’s needs and seek a voluntary agreement. This illustrates recognition respect for autonomy, while admiration for the teammate’s honesty would be a different, evaluative attitude.
summaries.summary: The entry treats respect as a family of related attitudes and practices rather than a single simple response. Respect may consist in complying with a rule, taking account of danger, honoring an institutional role, caring for something fragile, or valuing a person’s character. Philosophical analysis often distinguishes recognition respect, which gives an object appropriate weight in deliberation, from appraisal respect, which favorably evaluates character or conduct. The former is central to respect for persons. On the influential Kantian view, persons are rational and autonomous agents with dignity: their worth is unconditional, so they must not be treated merely as instruments for someone else’s purposes. This does not settle every issue. Philosophers disagree about the basis and scope of personhood, whether wrongdoers can lose their claim to respect, and whether respect requires only restraint or also assistance, protection, and support for autonomy. Other accounts argue that animals, living beings, or nature have moral standing. The entry also distinguishes recognition self-respect, grounded in one’s equal status and agency, from evaluative self-respect, grounded in one’s assessment of one’s character and conduct. Kant presents self-respect as a duty, while Rawls emphasizes social conditions that make self-respect possible. Across these debates, respect remains connected to equality, rights, autonomy, justice, identity, and opposition to humiliation.
key_ideas: Respect has cognitive, emotional, motivational, behavioral, valuational, and normative dimensions; no single dimension explains every use of the term.
The recognition/appraisal distinction separates owed consideration from favorable judgment, although philosophers debate whether it captures every form, including reverence and care.
Kant’s influential account holds that persons possess dignity and must not be treated merely as means, regardless of merit, status, or achievement.
Disputes concern who counts as a person, what grounds moral respect, whether respect can be forfeited, and whether respectful duties are only negative or also positive.
Some philosophers extend moral standing beyond persons to animals, living things, ecosystems, or nature, while others give persons a distinctive or higher status.
Self-respect includes recognition of one’s equal standing and agency, and its development can depend on social institutions and relationships.
summaries.why_it_matters: Respect influences how moral rules become lived relationships. It can limit coercion, deception, humiliation, exploitation, and the reduction of people to their usefulness. It also raises questions about institutions: laws and public practices can recognize equal standing, or they can communicate that some people matter less. The distinction between basic respect and earned admiration helps explain why condemning conduct need not mean declaring a person worthless. Examining respect therefore clarifies disagreements in ethics, political philosophy, health care, education, environmental ethics, and everyday interaction.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which a subject attends to an object, judges its significance, values it in an appropriate way, and is disposed to respond accordingly.
Respect that gives appropriate weight to a fact about an object when deciding how to act; it need not involve admiration.
Positive assessment of someone’s character or conduct by standards they may meet to greater or lesser degrees.
The idea that a person has unconditional, non-comparable worth rather than merely a price based on usefulness.
The capacity to set ends, govern oneself through reason, and take responsibility for one’s conduct.
The idea that something matters morally in its own right and may therefore deserve direct moral concern.
A form of self-regard involving appropriate appreciation of one’s worth and a disposition to protect it.
A moral theory associated here with Kant that gives central importance to treating persons as ends rather than merely as tools.

questions_to_think_about: Does equal moral respect require identical treatment, or can different needs justify different treatment?
Can punishment respect a wrongdoer, or does punishment necessarily conflict with respect?
If respect is grounded in rational autonomy, what follows for humans with severely diminished capacities or for nonhuman beings?
Can a person recognize another’s status without emotionally valuing that person?
Should social institutions be judged partly by whether they support or undermine citizens’ self-respect?

summaries.example: Jordan strongly disagrees with a friend’s plan for a school club. Jordan listens, asks what the friend means, and replies without mocking them. This is not the same as admiration, because Jordan does not think the plan is especially good. It is recognition respect: giving the person’s view enough attention to consider it seriously. If the club has a rule about taking turns, following that rule is another kind of respect. The two actions may look similar, but they involve different reasons.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of respect begins with an ordinary idea: some people and things should not be ignored, dismissed, or treated carelessly. Yet “respect” can name several different responses. Following a rule is one kind of respectful behavior. Showing deference to a social role is another. Thinking highly of a person because of admirable character is appraisal respect. Recognition respect instead means giving appropriate weight to someone or something when deciding how to act; it may be owed even when we do not like or admire the object. The most influential philosophical discussion concerns respect for persons. Kant’s view says that persons have dignity because of their rational and autonomous nature. Therefore, a person must not be treated merely as a useful object, even though people can sometimes cooperate and serve one another’s purposes. Philosophers debate whether this respect is owed to every human being, whether it can be forfeited, and whether it requires only avoiding abuse or also helping protect autonomy and rights. There is also debate about extending moral respect to animals and nature. Self-respect is another major theme. It involves valuing oneself, taking responsibility for one’s life, and resisting humiliation or servility. Some accounts focus on a duty to oneself; others emphasize the social conditions needed for people to develop and maintain self-respect.
key_ideas: Respect is not just being polite. It can involve attention, judgment, feelings, motivation, and action.
Recognition respect and appraisal respect are different: one is often owed, while the other is usually earned or lost.
Kant argued that all persons have dignity and should never be treated only as tools for another person’s goals.
Philosophers disagree about whether every human being is owed respect, what makes someone a person, and whether serious wrongdoing can remove a person’s claim to respect.
Some thinkers argue that animals, living things, or nature also deserve moral consideration.
Self-respect can be shaped by one’s own choices and by how families, schools, laws, and communities treat people.
summaries.why_it_matters: Respect affects trust, disagreement, education, work, law, medicine, and political life. It gives us a way to distinguish criticism from contempt and cooperation from manipulation. It also helps explain why unfair institutions can harm people even without a personal insult: they may signal that some members have lower standing. Studying respect does not provide one universally accepted answer to every conflict, but it helps us identify what is at stake and why reasonable people may disagree.

important_terms.definition: Taking a person, rule, tradition, or other object seriously and responding in an appropriate way.
Respect shown by giving something proper weight when deciding what to do.
Respect that means thinking highly of someone because of their character, conduct, or achievements.
A person’s special worth, understood by many philosophers as not depending on popularity, success, or usefulness.
The ability to make choices, guide one’s actions, and take responsibility for them.
Respect for oneself: seeing oneself as valuable and resisting treatment that is degrading.
The idea that something matters morally for its own sake, not only because it helps someone else.

questions_to_think_about: Why might respecting someone be different from admiring them?
Does treating everyone equally always show respect, or can fairness require different treatment?
If a person breaks a serious rule, what respect, if any, is still owed to them?
Can a society damage people’s self-respect even when no one directly insults them?
What reasons might support respecting nature for more than its usefulness to humans?
